children.text: The HIP-G Proximal Femur Nail is an intramedullary nail system for treatment of fractures, revisions, and tumor stabilizations in the proximal femur, including combined injury patterns affecting the shaft area (long nails)

Key system concepts include a two-portal proximal fixation concept for rotational stability intra- and post-operatively, and a DyCon® screw pair intended to function as a dynamically controlled force carrier system in the femoral neck/head

Controlled dynamization is provided via the inferior DyCon® Set Screw engaging the groove of the Lag Screw, allowing scalable lateral dynamization (0mm static to 10mm dynamic+) while inhibiting medial migration via full contact area between screws

conditions requiring physician risk/benefit consideration, including
dependence on patient bone quality for adequate fixation until bony healing occurs
excessive stresses on bone/implant (e.g., severe obesity) or degenerative diseases
interfering systemic conditions such as infection
demonstrated allergy or foreign body sensitivity to any implant materials
proximal femur landmarks relevant to trochanteric entry nailing include
inferior femoral neck cortex (Adam’s arch/calar region) is a critical zone when planning inferior trajectories near the neck cortex
abductors (gluteus medius/minimus) attach to the greater trochanter and influence trochanteric tenderness and lateral approach dissection planes
iliopsoas insertion on the lesser trochanter can contribute to flexion/external rotation of proximal fragments in subtrochanteric patterns
short external rotators and gluteal musculature contribute to deforming forces and can complicate reduction in unstable patterns
hip capsule and iliofemoral/pubo-femoral/ischiofemoral ligaments contribute to hip stability and can limit reduction maneuvers
ligamentum teres contributes minimally to adult femoral head perfusion compared with retinacular vessels
sciatic nerve is at risk with excessive traction, aggressive posterior retraction, or malpositioning
superior gluteal nerve is relevant to proximal lateral dissection planes and abductor function
lateral femoral cutaneous nerve may be irritated with proximal lateral incisions and retraction
medial femoral circumflex artery (deep branch) supplies most of the femoral head via retinacular vessels
intracapsular displacement and excessive manipulation can threaten perfusion in femoral neck–adjacent injuries
obtain pelvic overview imaging and longitudinal imaging of the affected femur with the hip joint in a/p and (if feasible) lateral projections
Position patient supine on a table that allows unobstructed fluoroscopy and a freely adjustable extension device via foot fixation
position the healthy leg rotated to the opposite side with ~90° hip/knee flexion and supported
secure the arm on the affected side across the body
lateral position is possible (e.g., shaft fractures), acknowledging potentially more difficult proximal reduction
Localize incision using fluoroscopic marking for trochanter access
in a/p, place a drill-wire transverse to the body axis resting on the trochanter tip in projection

images.caption: in a/p, place a drill-wire transverse to the body axis resting on the trochanter tip in projection; mark height on lateral thigh

children.text: in lateral, place drill-wire centrally in femoral axis and mark longitudinally above the horizontal line
Perform a proximal lateral incision for trochanter entry
create ~2–3cm incision starting ~2–4cm proximal to the trochanteric apex (soft tissue dependent)
sharply split fascia longitudinally; elevate musculature to palpate the anterior-to-posterior trochanteric ridge
divide the ridge into thirds; usual entry point is at the junction of the anterior third and middle third

images.caption: divide the ridge into thirds; usual entry point is at the junction of the anterior third and middle third

children.text: achieve closed reduction (length, axis, rotation) under fluoroscopy

images.caption: in a/p, place a drill-wire transverse to the body axis resting on the trochanter tip in projection; mark height on lateral thigh

children.text: open reduction is required if displaced subtrochanteric patterns are irreducible.
place drill-wire centrally in the femoral axis (check valgus path in A/P)

images.caption: divide the ridge into thirds; usual entry point is at the junction of the anterior third and middle third

children.text: use parallel holes in the conical sleeve if repositioning is needed
advance tissue protection sleeve to the trochanter
ream over the drill-wire until the depth stop hits the sleeve

images.caption: open the medullary canal over the drill-wire with the opening reamer through the sleeve until the depth stop contacts the sleeve

children.text: if the canal is narrow, use a ball-tip guide wire and ream over it
match nail to length, diameter, and CCD angle (120°/125°/130°)
attach nail to targeting arm and **double-check the holding bolt is fully tightened**
insert K-wire sleeves through the master sleeve until they firmly contact the **lateral cortex**

images.caption: insert K-wire sleeves into corresponding tissue protection sleeves and advance fully until contact with lateral femoral cortex

children.text: center the femoral head in lateral view
drill wire to a central position
final tip should be **~5mm** below the bone-cartilage transition in A/P view

images.caption: final tip should be ~5mm below the transition of bony zone into cartilage

children.text: place the inferior wire parallel to the first
anchor it **5-10mm shorter** than the superior wire
remove superior K-wire sleeve (keep inferior wire in for stability)
drill over the superior wire until the stop is reached
align markings on the driver with the sleeve
final positioning is adjustable in 1.6mm increments
replace inferior K-wire sleeve with the set screw sleeve
it will automatically "push off" the driver at the 5mm dynamization depth
insert via the nail holding bolt pathway
tighten until it engages the lag screw groove

images.caption: the axial set screw must rest in the groove of the lag screw and must not be backed out

children.text: drill with Ø4.2mm bit through the sleeve (ratchet seated on bone)

images.caption: drill with calibrated Ø4.2mm drill for Ø5mm locking screws to the medial inner cortex

children.text: add length for the medial cortex and insert Ø5mm screw
use the lower position of the elongated hole
remove sleeves and unscrew the nail holding bolt only **after** all locking is complete
verify final implant position and screw lengths via fluoroscopy before wound closure
used only if nail extension or scar tissue protection is required
12° anteversion of femoral neck (as described for system concept/rotation control)
two proximal portals for lag screw (superior) and set screw (inferior) trajectories
self-retaining mechanism for DyCon® Set Screw (as described)
short and intermediate nails use average femoral antecurvature of 1100mm

children.text: controlled lateral dynamization control (0–10mm) while inhibiting medial migration via screw-to-screw contact
can be used universally when needed/preferred
can be used alone or with dycon® set screw
if used alone, medial movement of lag screw is blocked and lateral movement is free depending on remaining groove length of lag screw
